content.p: In the first week of December 1982, soldiers from a notorious army unit, the Kaibiles, came to a hamlet called Las Dos Erres, in the northern department of Petén, and killed most of the people who lived there. The killing went on for about three days. The bodies were thrown down a well and into the fields around the village, and the village was then razed.

The number of dead is still disputed. A Guatemalan court that convicted the first group of soldiers in 2011 counted 201 identified victims. Amnesty International and the US National Security Archive have written of 250 or more. The BBC reported in 2018 that more than 200 people died. Those figures are set out below, each with the source that gave it.

The massacre belongs to the civil war that ran from 1960 to 1996. A UN-backed truth commission, which reported in 1999, estimated that at least 200,000 people were killed in that war, and it attributed 93 percent of the killings to the security forces, according to the BBC. Amnesty International, citing the same commission, put the number of mass killings by the security forces at more than 600.

Dos Erres sat in Petén, the northernmost department of Guatemala, and the National Security Archive describes it as a tiny settlement. During the brief rule of General Efraín Ríos Montt, who took power in a coup, the army ran what ProPublica called a search-and-destroy campaign against rural villages believed to shelter guerrilla fighters. Witnesses described the campaign as a scorched-earth effort to remove communities that supported the insurgents.

Two months before the killings, guerrillas ambushed an army patrol in the area and killed 21 soldiers, according to the BBC. ICE, which later described the events in a press release, said the attackers also took more than 20 military rifles. The Kaibiles who came to Dos Erres were looking for those weapons. The Kaibiles were the army's special forces, and a 1980 US Defense Intelligence Agency report, which the National Security Archive published, placed their training centre at La Pólvora in Petén.

Accounts differ on the date. The CEJIL case page places the events on 6, 7 and 8 December 1982. The National Security Archive says a Kaibil unit attacked the village on the morning of 6 December and that the killings continued over the next three days. Amnesty gives 5 December as the day the unit arrived. NBC News, citing court filings, says the attack began before dawn on 7 December.

The soldiers did not find the rifles, according to ICE, which says no weapons were recovered in the village. The Kaibiles separated the men from the women and children, and then questioned the villagers about the stolen guns. The BBC reported that the soldiers suspected the villagers of sympathising with the guerrillas, and that they killed the inhabitants anyway.

The methods are described in the same way across the pages that were opened. Villagers were beaten, shot, strangled or bludgeoned, and some were killed with sledgehammers, according to NBC News, which cited Reuters for that detail, and to the ICE release. Many women and girls were raped, according to CEJIL, ICE and Amnesty. Children were among those thrown into the village well, which had not been finished. The bodies that were not thrown into the well were left in nearby fields, according to the National Security Archive.

The unit did not all act alike. ProPublica reports that Favio Pinzón, a cook who had failed Kaibil training, later became the first repentant soldier to give a first-hand account of the massacre, and that another soldier described dragging residents to the well. ProPublica also reports that a deputy commander, Oscar Ovidio Ramírez Ramos, took a three-year-old boy home after the killings, and that a soldier named Santos López Alonzo raised a five-year-old boy who had been taken from the village. Both boys survived. ProPublica also describes an 11-year-old survivor, Hernández, who saw some of the killing and escaped while the soldiers were taking other children and women away to be killed in the hills. The search for the first boy led to the 2017 documentary Finding Oscar, which the BBC mentions.

For a long time the killings went unpunished. The case was first investigated in 1994, according to the BBC and Amnesty International. The National Security Archive says a team of forensic anthropologists began exhuming the village in 1995, and that the investigation did not move forward for years. Amnesty said dozens of appeals filed by the defence kept the case in the courts for years after it was opened. An earlier trial, in 2004, ended with a verdict against one officer and 13 soldiers, but NBC reports that the verdict was overturned on appeal.

The exhumation recovered the remains of 171 victims, NBC reports, and at least 67 of them were children under 12. In 2001 President Alfonso Portillo acknowledged that 226 people had been killed and that the state was responsible, and he awarded relatives $1.8 million in compensation, the BBC reports. A 2009 decision from the Inter-American Court ruled that the state must act in the case.

The US government's own records became part of the case. The National Security Archive obtained declassified US documents on the Kaibiles and the massacre. One US Embassy assessment, cited by the archive, concluded that the party most likely responsible was the Guatemalan army, and, in the archive's account, US officials saw the army as the sole force able to carry out an operation of that organisation.

The trial began in July 2011, with four former soldiers in the dock. The BBC described them as members of the Kaibiles, the special forces unit, and identified them as Carlos Antonio Carias, Manuel Pop Sun, Reyes Collin Gualip and Daniel Martinez. All four denied involvement. The BBC reported that the local human rights group CALDH called the trial historic, the first of its kind to involve former soldiers.

In August 2011 the court convicted all four. Pop Sun, Collin Gualip and Martinez each received 6,060 years, which NBC described as 30 years for each of 201 victims plus 30 years for crimes against humanity. Carias, a former second lieutenant whom prosecutors said was in charge of a military base near Dos Erres, was sentenced to 6,066 years, with an extra six years for stealing the victims' belongings. The sentences are largely symbolic, since Guatemalan law caps time in prison at 50 years. ProPublica reports that Carias helped plan the raid and covered up the evidence afterwards.

Survivors wept outside the court when the sentences were read, and red rose petals were laid in the shape of the word "justice" on the ground, NBC reported. Relatives of the accused shouted that the court had been biased. Carias called the sentence unjust and said he would risk his life again for the army.
content.h2: Pimentel Ríos and the wider cases
content.p: Pedro Pimentel Ríos was not in the first group. He had been arrested in California in May 2010 and deported to Guatemala in July 2011, a month before the four others were convicted, according to Amnesty and ProPublica. ProPublica reports that he had been taken to Panama after the massacre to serve as an instructor at the School of the Americas, and that the Guatemalan army gave him a commendation medal in 1985.

In March 2012 a three-judge panel convicted him and sentenced him to 6,060 years. He told the court he had not taken part and that he had been in Guatemala City on the day of the killings. Two admitted perpetrators identified him as one of the killers, a 2012 wire report said. The defence said he was in Guatemala City that day. The Amnesty release on his case described him as the fifth former soldier convicted for the massacre.

The trial of Ríos Montt, the former head of state, was a parallel effort. Ríos Montt was under house arrest from January 2012 while awaiting a possible trial for genocide, a 2012 wire report said. ProPublica reported in May 2012 that a Guatemalan court had decided he could also be tried as the person behind the Dos Erres operation. He died in April 2018, aged 91, while on trial for genocide, the BBC reported.

Several of the men who took part were living in the United States, and US authorities brought cases against them, mostly for lying about their pasts when they applied for citizenship or residence. Gilberto Jordán was arrested by immigration agents in Palm Beach County, Florida, in May 2010. ICE says he had become a naturalised American citizen in 1999 and had denied, on his application, that he had served in the military. In July 2010 he pleaded guilty and admitted he had been a Kaibil at Dos Erres. He also admitted that the first person he killed there was a baby, whom he threw into the well. A federal judge gave him ten years in September 2010 and cancelled his naturalisation.

Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes, a former commander of the special forces unit, was arrested in Alberta, Canada, on 18 January 2011 on US charges of naturalisation fraud. The National Security Archive reports that a US Justice Department prosecutor told the Calgary Sun the extradition request concerned the fraud allegations and not the massacre. The archive's release does not say what happened to that extradition request.

Santos López Alonzo was deported from the United States and arrested in Houston after a re-entry. ProPublica reports that in 1999 he had confessed to a prosecutor that he had abducted a five-year-old boy from Dos Erres and had taken part in the massacre. ICE says he was removed to Guatemala on 10 August 2016 and sentenced on 22 November 2018 to 5,160 years. The BBC reported the same day that he was sentenced to 30 years for each of 171 killings and to a further 30 years for the murder of a girl who had first survived the raid.

On 7 November 2023 a court in Guatemala, the Tribunal de Mayor Riesgo E, acquitted three former soldiers who had been charged with murder and crimes against humanity over the killings. Prensa Libre named them as Gilberto Jordán, Alfonso Bulux and José Mardoqueo Ortiz, and ordered their release. The newspaper reported that six other soldiers had been convicted in various Dos Erres cases since 2011.

One of the judges, Edy de León Morales, said during the reading of the verdict that the evidence against the accused was not certain. Prensa Libre reported that relatives of the victims reacted with cries and sobs, and that they described the verdict as corrupt. Ortiz had been deported from the United States in 2021 and handed to Guatemalan justice. Jordán had been removed to Guatemala in a flight that ICE announced in a release dated March 2020.

The acquittal did not close the case. The National Security Archive says that the search for the remaining fugitives continues. ProPublica identified one senior officer, Batres, who was accused of raping a young girl in front of her family and who remained at large when that article was published in 2012.
content.h2: Accountability and what is still disputed
content.p: Amnesty International welcomed the convictions in 2012 but said that the soldiers convicted had addressed only a tiny fraction of the crimes of the war. Its statement said that "higher ranking officers who were responsible have still to be brought to justice." The state's responsibility had already been acknowledged in 2001, when Portillo spoke of 226 deaths.

The figures are where the sources disagree. The 201 figure is the count of identified victims used at the 2011 sentencing, according to NBC News and ProPublica. The 171 figure is the number of remains recovered in the exhumation, per NBC. Amnesty and the National Security Archive use 250 or more; the BBC used "more than 200" in 2018, and in 2011 it wrote of more than 220. The start date is also contested: between 5 and 8 December, depending on the source.

Survivors testified at the trial, according to Amnesty International, and the National Security Archive supplied declassified US records to Guatemalan prosecutors. ProPublica's account names several more soldiers and officers, among them Batres, whom it describes as still at large.
